title: A taste that can't be told
hookLine: Dhruva can't find a word before Vishnu; the sutras on a love that can't be told
carry: bhakti can't be told, only tasted

cards: Year one met Dhruva, the five-year-old prince pushed off his father's lap, who went into the forest and held Vishnu in his heart for months.
Then the inner vision vanished, he opened his eyes, and Vishnu was standing in front of him. The Bhagavata says the boy gazed as if drinking him in.
He longed to praise him, and couldn't find a single word, until Vishnu touched his cheek with the conch and the praise poured out. Hold that boy in mind: full to the brim, and speechless.
Today the Narada Bhakti Sutras try to say what love itself is like, and they start by admitting they can't.

teach.b: The nature of love, the sutras say, cannot be told. Anirvacaniya. Then the comparison: it's like the tasting of someone who cannot speak.
The taste is completely real; it just can't get out in words.
It shows itself in a vessel fit for it: not everywhere at once, not on command, but in a particular person, at a particular time, the way it filled a small boy in a forest.
Then the sutras try anyway, with a string of qualities. It is free of the qualities that color ordinary feeling. It is free of wanting something back.
It grows every moment. It doesn't break off. It is subtler than the subtle.
And it is a matter of experience, not of theory. The things we like wear down with use. The sutras say this love does the opposite: the longer it runs, the more of it there is.

teach.h: SEE ONLY THAT, HEAR ONLY THAT.
teach.b: Having gained it, they see only that, hear only that, speak only of that, think only of that.
That's why bhakti in Hinduism is handed on by singing, stories and company more than by argument: you can't explain a taste, but you can share the plate.

Look back at the week: Tuladhara's honest scale, the renouncer who keeps working, Narada's monkey face, Narada in sorrow before Sanatkumara, Narada the servant boy among singers, Ajamila's ripple, and a boy struck speechless.
Tomorrow, the last pages: the people who have this love.

how: Devotional teachers quote the sutras' image of a taste that a person who cannot speak cannot describe, to explain why bhakti is passed on through singing, stories and company rather than argument.

o: love that can't be told, and grows every moment
a love that can be fully put into words
a feeling that fades as you get used to it

games.q: a taste that can't be told — tap the pairs.
p: they see and hear only that

s: the sutras give a full, exact definition of love itself
they say its nature cannot be told, like a taste for someone who cannot speak.
the sutras say this love grows every moment
pratikshana-vardhamana: increasing moment by moment, and never breaking off.
the sutras say this love shows itself in everyone at once
they say it shows itself somewhere, in a vessel fit for it.

games.q: you've been asked to explain the love the sutras describe. what do the sutras themselves do first?
o: admit it cannot be told, like a taste for one who cannot speak.
say it can't be experienced at all.
games.why: they start by saying it cannot be told. then they try anyway: free of wanting, growing every moment, subtler than the subtle, a matter of experience.

practice: Bring back a moment when you were deeply happy with someone or something you love: the light, the sound, the feeling in the chest.
Each time a word tries to describe it, let the word go and go back to the taste, no commentary, no captions. If you pray, you can rest in God the same way, without words.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. In the sutras, a love that can't be told, like a taste for someone who cannot speak, and it grows every moment.

orig.note: Sanskrit anirvacanīya, what cannot be told or put into words: the sutras' first word on the nature of love.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti can't be told, only tasted. Like Dhruva, sometimes you just have to be there. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Narada Bhakti Sutras 51–55 (love cannot be told; like the tasting of one who cannot speak; shows itself in a fit vessel; its qualities; having gained it, one sees, hears, speaks and thinks only of it)
